idiom_name: GORM has-many with FullSaveAssociations and Select(clause.Associations)
implementation_notes: GORM treats the child as an association of the parent: db.Create(&order) inserts the order and its []OrderLine in one transaction, db.Session(&gorm.Session{FullSaveAssociations: true}).Save(&order) rewrites the lines on update, and db.Select(clause.Associations).Delete(&order) deletes them with the parent, optionally backstopped by a constraint:OnDelete:CASCADE tag. The child has no repository - only the parent's repository method is public. GORM's default update touches only foreign-key references, so FullSaveAssociations is what makes the dependent mapping complete.
pitfalls: A plain Save only upserts foreign keys for existing associations: children removed from the slice survive in the table unless FullSaveAssociations (or an explicit delete) is used.
Select(clause.Associations).Delete needs a non-zero primary key in the passed struct - with a bare &Order{} GORM deletes the parents but silently leaves the children behind.
Without Omit/Select discipline a Create cascades into whatever happens to be attached to the slice, including objects loaded from another query.

variants.name: Hand-written repository over database/sql
variants.idiom_name: repository method that deletes and re-inserts the child rows in one transaction
variants.implementation_notes: Without an ORM the dependent mapping is a repository method: begin a transaction, replace all child rows for the parent, insert the new set, commit; loading joins the child rows for the parents fetched in the same query. This is the common Go style and it keeps the child type without a repository of its own (often unexported), at the cost of writing the replacement by hand and keeping every other caller away from the child table.
pitfalls: The transaction must cover delete and insert: a failed insert after the delete would leave the parent without its lines.
Reading child rows only through the parent query keeps the contract; adding an OrderLineRepository re-opens a second write path and breaks the aggregate.
